title: PRMT7 restricts CD8+ T cells expansion via the NF-ΚB pathway
abstract:
Nature Communications, Published online: 06 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-77155-2

Cytotoxic T cells (CTL) are successfully employed in tumour therapy but understanding how their expansion and effector function is regulated might result in further improvements. Here the authors show by a T-cell-specific deletion of Prmt7 and by developing a PRMT7-targeting PROTAC degrader that PRMT7 is a negative regulator of the NF-κB pathway in CTL, removing of which improves anti-tumour function of CTL.
headline: Blocking a protein called PRMT7 makes immune cells fight cancer better.
why_it_matters: Cancer immunotherapy using engineered immune cells has shown promise, but many patients don't respond well enough. This discovery identifies a molecular brake that weakens these cells, and removing it could make them more powerful fighters against tumors. This could lead to better treatments for patients whose cancers currently resist therapy.
key_findings: PRMT7 is a protein that acts like a brake on cytotoxic T cells (CTL — immune cells trained to kill cancer cells), preventing them from multiplying and attacking tumors effectively.
When researchers genetically removed PRMT7 from T cells in mice, the cells multiplied more and fought cancer better, shrinking tumors more successfully.
PRMT7 works by blocking a pathway called NF-κB (a cellular communication system that tells cells to grow and become active). Removing PRMT7 turns this pathway back on.
The team created a new drug-like molecule (called a PROTAC degrader) that can destroy PRMT7 in the body, offering a potential therapeutic approach that doesn't require genetic editing.
methods_snapshot: Researchers used genetically modified mice where the PRMT7 gene was deleted specifically in T cells, then tested how well these modified cells fought tumors. They also designed and tested a new molecule that chemically destroys PRMT7 protein to see if it had the same effect, mimicking what a future drug might do.

glossary.definition: A protein in cells that acts as a chemical modifier, tagging other proteins to change how they work; in this case, it dampens immune cell activity.
White blood cells trained by the immune system to recognize and kill cancer cells or infected cells.
A cellular communication network inside cells that receives signals telling the cell to grow, divide, and become active; it's like an on switch for cell activity.
A synthetic molecule designed to find and destroy a specific protein inside cells, acting like a targeted search-and-destroy weapon.
Genetically removing a gene from only one type of cell (here, T cells) while leaving it intact in all other cell types.

cancer_types: Not specified — study is foundational research on immune mechanism, applicable broadly to cancers treated with T-cell therapy
limitations: The study was conducted primarily in laboratory mice and cell cultures, so it's unclear whether blocking PRMT7 will be as effective or safe in human patients. The new drug-like molecule (PROTAC) is still in early development and would need extensive testing before use in humans.
